atoms.text: Washington, D.C., is famous for its beautiful cherry blossom trees that spread throughout the whole city. In springtime, the trees bloom, and vast parts of the city shine in a mesmerizing pink for a couple of weeks. But why are there so many trees, and how did they get there in the first place? The answer to these questions involves many people, but two women in particular: Mrs Eliza Ruhamah Scidmore and First Lady Helen Herron Taft. These exceptional and determined women created a botanical symbol of cultural exchange and international friendship.

These exceptional and determined women created a botanical symbol of cultural exchange and international friendship.

atoms.text: In the late 19th century, Eliza Ruhamah Scidmore had the idea to plant many Japanese cherry blossom trees in Washington, D.C. She traveled to Japan several times and was astonished by the beauty of the Japanese cherry trees. For many years, Mrs Scidmore tried to gain public interest in her cherry blossom tree project, but her attempts remained unsuccessful. Eventually, in 1909, her efforts began to bear fruit when Mrs Scidmore wrote a letter to First Lady Helen Herron Taft. She explained her landscaping ideas to plant cherry blossom trees close to the governmental district in Washington, D.C. Mrs Taft responded: “I have taken the matter up and am promised the trees, but I thought perhaps it would be best to make an avenue of them, extending down to the turn in the road.”

As a result, she became a strong advocate for Mrs Scidmore’s endeavour and immediately supported her plan. While Mrs Scidmore, a socialite, had the idea to install the cherry trees, Mrs Taft had the power to help her execute the plan. atoms.text: The original batch of trees from 1912 was a gift from Japan and its capital Tokyo to Washington, D.C. Japan wanted to strengthen its ties with the USA and offered the trees free of charge to the First Lady. This moment marked the beginning of the botanic diplomacy between the USA and Japan.<m-pink> The cherry trees have become an important symbol of the friendship and are seen as a diplomatic tool between the USA and Japan.</m-pink> <m-blue>In 1915, the USA sent flowering dogwood trees to Japan as a sign of their gratitude.</m-blue> Thereby, a continuous cycle of botanical exchange was established between the two countries.
atoms.sound: The original batch of trees from 1912 was a gift from Japan and its capital Tokyo to Washington, DC.  Japan wanted to strengthen its ties with the USA and offered the trees free of charge to the First Lady. This moment marked the beginning of the botanic diplomacy between the USA and Japan. The cherry trees have become an important symbol of the friendship and are seen as a diplomatic tool between the USA and Japan. In 1915, the USA sent flowering dogwood trees to Japan as a sign of their gratitude. Thereby, a continuous cycle of botanical exchange was established between the two countries.

atoms.text: Over the years, Japan and the USA have been sending trees or cuttings of trees back and forth as a symbol of friendship and support. <m-blue>In 1981, many cherry trees in Japan were destroyed due to heavy flooding.</m-blue> <m-purple>This was when the USA returned some original trees to their homeland. The USA cut branches from the original batch and sent them back to Japan so that they could reforest their own cherry trees.</m-purple> Thus, the trees underwent a complete cycle and fulfilled their role as diplomatic agents.
atoms.sound: Over the years, Japan and the USA have been sending trees or cuttings of trees back and forth as a symbol of friendship and support. In 1981, many cherry trees in Japan were destroyed due to heavy flooding. This was when the USA returned some original trees to their homeland. The USA cut branches from the original batch and sent them back to Japan so that they could reforest their own cherry trees. Thus, the trees underwent a complete cycle and fulfilled their role as diplomatic agents.

atoms.text: In conclusion, the cherry blossoms in Washington, D.C. are an exceptional symbol of female determination, stamina, cultural exchange and international friendship.
